summary:
Workplace Insight reports on Logitech's inaugural Ctrl Tomorrow Study, a global survey arguing that a person's sense of control over workplace technology is linked to wellbeing, productivity and openness to technological change. The study describes a divide between people who feel confident and in command of their tools and those who feel overwhelmed or frustrated.

Key findings: 77 percent agreed people who feel more in control of their technology get more out of life, and around three in five said technology problems affect their mood after work and their sense of control over personal life. Poor or hard-to-use technology produced frustration, anxiety or anger for 64 percent, while 46 percent felt helpless, embarrassed, exhausted or behind. Conversely 52 percent said control over technology let them accomplish something they thought was beyond them.

Logitech created a Ctrl Score measuring how deliberately people construct their tech setup, their confidence in and openness to new tools, and whether they see technology as enabling or limiting. Only 30 percent showed high agency and 10 percent were classed as fully in command.

On automation, 41 percent said time freed by technology handling routine tasks would go to wellbeing, mental health or work-life balance, more so among lower Ctrl Scores. Physical hardware still matters: nearly two-thirds felt most in control interacting with physical devices and 42 percent rely on them more than five years ago. Gamers reported high confidence, with 81 percent saying gaming increased real-world confidence and reduced anxiety.

Geographic splits were wide. 61 percent globally said technology helps them fulfil personal potential, rising to 80 percent in China and 78 percent in Brazil versus 45 percent in France, 55 percent US, 56 percent Germany. Technology optimism averaged 74 percent globally, 84 percent in India and Brazil, 60 percent in France. AI excitement: 41 percent India, 23 percent Switzerland, 16 percent US, 15 percent UK, 13 percent Australia. CEO Hanneke Faber framed control as the deciding factor in the age of AI.
